# Embeddings: Words as Coordinates {#sec-embeddings}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain the distributional hypothesis and turn it into a matrix, then into coordinates;
- reweight co-occurrence counts with PPMI, which compares the observed probability of a pair with what an independence model predicts and sets negative PMI values to zero;
- compress the result with truncated SVD — the method that keeps a table's strongest patterns and drops the rest — and say what each step fixes;
- write skip-gram with negative sampling from scratch and explain how its two vector tables are learned together under a logistic loss;
- choose between word2vec, GloVe, fastText and doc2vec for a stated problem, and defend it;
- examine three properties of the space: vectors not being spread evenly over directions (anisotropy), the effect of frequency on the representation, and cosine similarity reflecting relations broader than synonymy;
- explain why a static embedding's representation does not change with context, and discuss why the contextual representations of @sec-transformers are needed.

## The problem, in one sentence

@sec-text-as-data ended in an uncomfortable place. Document vectors worked,
but one-hot word vectors shared no similarity between words at all.

Every word was a one-hot column, so `pump`, `pumps` and `impeller` were three
mutually orthogonal directions — each as unrelated to the others as `pump` is
to `Wednesday`. Cosine similarity between any two distinct words was exactly
zero. By construction. Always.

A good representation should be able to tell three relations apart:
morphological closeness like `pump`–`pumps`, semantic or functional closeness
like `pump`–`impeller`, and unrelatedness like `pump`–`Wednesday`.

An example shows what follows from that. In a linear model that uses only word
counts, `pump` and `pumps` are separate features. Suppose your training data
contains *the pump failed* and your test data contains *the pumps failed*. The
weights learned for `the` and `failed` can be used; the weight learned for
`pump`, however, does not carry over to the `pumps` feature by itself.

::: {#gloss-embedding .column-margin .term-gloss}
**embedding** — a learned numerical representation of a unit. In this chapter
we mostly represent words with dense vectors of relatively few dimensions; in
distributional methods, words used in similar contexts can end up close together
in that space. Think of it as giving every word a set of map coordinates. [↩](#term-embedding){.term-back}
:::

In this chapter we move from the one-hot representation, which gives every word
its own axis, to one in which all words are represented with the same small
number of learned dimensions. In linear-algebra terms that means
[multiplying the one-hot vectors by a learned matrix]{.hl}.

For each word we get, say, 100 or 300 numbers, and we aim for words used in
similar ways to end up near each other. That short, **dense** vector is an
[embedding](#gloss-embedding){#term-embedding .term-ref}. In a dense vector most
components are usually non-zero; in the **sparse** count vectors of
@sec-text-as-data most components were zero.

**Three kinds of embedding, one chapter.** The word "embedding" is used for
three different things, and separating them now makes the rest of the chapter
easier:

| Kind | Example | Does the same word get the same vector everywhere? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Static word embedding** | word2vec, GloVe, fastText | Yes — one vector per word form, whatever the context |
| **Contextual token embedding** | BERT | No — each token's vector is computed from its context in the sequence given to the model; one word can consist of several tokens |
| **Sentence or document embedding** | SBERT and its relatives | Not the question: one vector for the whole sentence or document |

: The three things "embedding" can mean {tbl-colwidths="[28,26,46]"}

[This chapter is about static word embeddings.]{.hl} It also gives a short
introduction to document vectors. Contextual representations are covered in
@sec-transformers, and the use of sentence and document representations in
retrieval in @sec-retrieval.

**Two reading layers.** The chapter is long; on a first read this spine is
enough:

- **On a first read:** the distributional hypothesis → co-occurrence →
  word2vec → cosine → GloVe and fastText → the limits of static embeddings.
- **Deep dive (second read):** the mathematics of PPMI and SVD → the gradient
  of negative sampling → the relationship between SGNS and PMI → the
  anisotropy and bias measurements.

Most of the derivations in the second layer sit in collapsible *Deep dive*
boxes; the main line is complete without opening them.

**What we will look at.** We first build the space from counts; on a small
example every step can be checked by hand. Then we write skip-gram with negative
sampling from scratch, gradients included, and examine how that method relates
to PMI. Finally we look at what embeddings are used for, at their geometric
properties, and at the limits of a representation that does not change with
context. On a first read you can skip the collapsible *Deep dive* boxes and the
from-scratch implementation code.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: the statistician's framing

One-hot encoding shows categories as separate coordinates. In some models that
use it, independent parameters are learned for each category. Representing
word–context interactions with two low-rank matrices, by contrast, gives those
interactions a shared structure. That structure can let what is learned from
similar distributions contribute to generalization. It should not be equated
with a saturated model or with hierarchical partial pooling in the technical
sense; the comparison is there for intuition only.
:::

## The distributional hypothesis

> *"You shall know a word by the company it keeps."* — J.R. Firth, 1957
> [@firth1957synopsis]

Firth was making a point about linguistic method; Zellig Harris had already
made the operational version of it [@harris1954distributional]. The claim is
that a substantial amount of semantic and functional information about a word
can be recovered from the distribution of contexts it appears in.

Put concretely: if two words keep appearing in the same slots —
`the ___ failed`, `replaced the ___`, `___ pressure dropped` — then their uses
are systematically similar.

This is not a theorem but a hypothesis that is tested against data. Sharing
similar contexts can help to identify topical or functional closeness. It does
not by itself identify synonymy: antonyms such as *hot* and *cold* share many
contexts too. Later in this chapter we look at that distinction with numerical
examples.

An important advantage of this approach is that it needs no hand-labelled
examples. The training signal is derived from the contexts in raw text. That
makes it possible to learn representations from large unlabelled corpora.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What does "similar" mean here?** Distributional similarity is not the same as
synonymy. `cat` and `dog` are the same kind of thing; `doctor` and `hospital`
are related; `hot` and `cold` are opposites that keep the same company. That
distinction comes back later in this chapter, when we read cosine similarity.
:::

## Count first: co-occurrence, PPMI, SVD

A count-based approach does three things. It counts the word–context pairs
inside a chosen context window (their co-occurrences), reweights the counts, and
approximates the resulting matrix with a low-rank structure. Following those
steps on a small example makes the later methods easier to understand.
Skip-gram with negative sampling has also been shown, under certain assumptions,
to implicitly factorize a matrix related to PMI, which is defined below
[@levy2014neural].

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The three steps in this section.**

1. **Count.** Which words appear in which contexts?
2. **Reweight.** Compare the observed pair frequency with the value expected
   from the marginal frequencies of the word and the context.
3. **Compress.** Represent the repeated patterns in fewer dimensions.
:::

Here is a corpus of ten sentences, small enough to check every number.

```python
import numpy as np

corpus = [
    "the king rules the castle",
    "the queen rules the castle",
    "the king eats an apple",
    "the queen eats a banana",
    "the royal castle is grand",
    "a banana is sweet fruit",
    "an apple is sweet fruit",
    "the man eats an apple",
    "the woman eats a banana",
    "the king and queen are royal",
]

tokens = [s.split() for s in corpus]
vocab = sorted({w for s in tokens for w in s})
idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
V = len(vocab)
print("sentences:", len(corpus), " vocabulary:", V)
print(vocab)
```

```text
sentences: 10  vocabulary: 19
['a', 'an', 'and', 'apple', 'are', 'banana', 'castle', 'eats', 'fruit', 'grand', 'is', 'king', 'man', 'queen', 'royal', 'rules', 'sweet', 'the', 'woman']
```

### Step 1 — count what appears near what

Here the context of a word consists of up to two tokens to its left and up to
two to its right, within the same sentence. The centre token is not part of its
own context. For every (centre word, context word) pair we add one to the
corresponding cell; because the window is symmetric, the pair in the opposite
direction is counted too, at its own centre position.

```python
W = 2
C = np.zeros((V, V))
for sent in tokens:
    for i, w in enumerate(sent):
        for j in range(max(0, i - W), min(len(sent), i + W + 1)):
            if i != j:
                C[idx[w], idx[sent[j]]] += 1
```

```text
### raw co-occurrence, a few rows
            eats   rules   royal   sweet     the  castle
king           1       1       0       0       4       0
queen          1       1       1       0       3       0
apple          2       0       0       1       0       0
banana         2       0       0       1       0       0
```

Already the structure is visible: `king` and `queen` have nearly the same
row, and so do `apple` and `banana`. That is the distributional hypothesis
working. The rows of $C$ *are* word vectors — 19-dimensional ones — and
unlike one-hots they are not orthogonal.

But they have chapter 2's disease.

```text
### the same problem as chapter 2: 'the' dominates
  the      total co-occurrences    22
  eats     total co-occurrences    16
  is       total co-occurrences    11
  queen    total co-occurrences    10
  king     total co-occurrences     9
  a        total co-occurrences     8
```

The largest count in the `king` row belongs to `the`. But `the` is frequent
around many words, so that high count cannot by itself be read as an association
specific to kings. Raw counts are affected by the association and also by how
frequent the words are overall.

### Step 2 — PPMI: from raw counts to unexpected co-occurrence

::: {#gloss-pointwise-mutual-information-pmi .column-margin .term-gloss}
**pointwise mutual information (PMI)** — the logarithm of the ratio between
the observed probability of a word–context pair and the product of its marginal
probabilities. It is positive for pairs seen more often than the independence
model expects and negative for pairs seen less often. [↩](#term-pointwise-mutual-information-pmi){.term-back}
:::

We want to ask: *do these two words co-occur more often than chance would
predict?* [Pointwise mutual information](#gloss-pointwise-mutual-information-pmi){#term-pointwise-mutual-information-pmi .term-ref} asks exactly that.

$$
\mathrm{PMI}(w, c) = \log \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w)\,P(c)}
$$

Read the fraction like this: the denominator ($P(w)\,P(c)$) is how often we
would *expect* the two words to land next to each other if they were placed
completely independently; the numerator ($P(w, c)$) is how often they
actually do. So PMI is nothing but the log of **observed ÷ expected**. Three
cases:

- **Ratio 1** — the observed probability of this pair equals the value the
  independence model predicts. Since $\log 1 = 0$, PMI is zero. That does not
  mean there is no semantic relationship between the words.
- **Ratio above 1** — they co-occur more often than expected; they *attract*.
  The log is positive.
- **Ratio below 1** — they co-occur less often than expected; they *avoid*
  each other. The log is negative.

Particularly for rare words, observing only a few co-occurrences may not be
enough to estimate a negative association reliably. [Positive PMI (PPMI)]{.hl}
sets negative PMI values to zero and so keeps only the pairs seen more often
than the independence model expects. That can be a useful representational
choice; it does not mean that every negative PMI value is meaningless.

$$
\mathrm{PPMI}(w, c) = \max\!\left(0,\ \log \frac{c_{wc}\, N}{c_{w\ast}\, c_{\ast c}}\right)
$$

Here $c_{wc}$ is how often the pair actually occurred, $c_{w\ast}$ is the row
total, $c_{\ast c}$ the column total, and $N$ the grand total of the matrix.
That fraction is doing something very simple, and it is worth seeing it with
actual numbers.

**Work one cell by hand.** We will run the formula on `apple`–`sweet`, but
first pin down where the four numbers come from, because all four are read
off the same matrix $C$:

- $c_{wc} = 1$ — how many times `apple` and `sweet` actually landed in each
  other's window. That is a single cell, visible in the table above.
- $c_{w\ast} = 7$ — the **sum of the `apple` row**, meaning "how many times
  was `apple` counted next to anything at all". `apple` occurs three times in
  the corpus, with 2, 3 and 2 neighbours respectively: $2 + 3 + 2 = 7$.
- $c_{\ast c} = 6$ — the same sum for `sweet`, down its **column**.
- $N = 144$ — the sum of every cell in the matrix: all the (word, neighbour)
  pairs counted in the corpus. You can check it by hand. Each token
  contributes one pair per neighbour in its window — 4 for a token in the
  middle of a sentence, 2 or 3 at the edges — so a five-token sentence yields
  14 pairs. The corpus has nine five-token sentences and one six-token
  sentence (18 pairs): $9 \times 14 + 18 = 144$.

Note that $N$ is not the 51 tokens in the corpus; it is the number of
*pairs*. All three probabilities — $P(w, c)$, $P(w)$ and $P(c)$ — are estimated
from the same pair table (the cell, the row sum and the column sum), so all
three are divided by how many pairs were counted, not how many tokens exist.

Now the actual question: if the two words were sprinkled through the text
completely independently, how many times would we *expect* them to land next
to each other?

$$
\frac{c_{\text{apple},\ast} \times c_{\ast,\text{sweet}}}{N}
= \frac{7 \times 6}{144} = 0.29
$$

We observed 1, which is $144 / 42 = 3.43$ times more than expected. PMI is
the log of that ratio: $\log 3.43 = 1.23$ — the value in the table.

Now do the same for `king`–`the`, which occurs **four** times — exactly four
times as often as `apple`–`sweet`. But `the` is everywhere: its column sums
to 22, and the `king` row sums to 9. The independence model predicts
$9 \times 22 / 144 = 1.38$ co-occurrences for this pair.

Put the two calculations side by side:

| | observed | expected | ratio | PMI |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `apple`–`sweet` | 1 | $7 \times 6 / 144 = 0.29$ | 3.43 | **1.23** |
| `king`–`the` | 4 | $9 \times 22 / 144 = 1.38$ | 2.91 | **1.07** |

: Raw count and frequency relative to the independence model {tbl-colwidths="[24,17,29,15,15]"}

The `apple`–`sweet` pair, observed once, gets the **higher** PMI because its
observed-to-expected ratio is larger. The expected count is 1.38 for
`king`–`the` and 0.29 for `apple`–`sweet`. Those expectations do not say how
much of what we observed is causally "explained"; PMI compares two relative
frequencies.

::: {.column-margin}
Think of a crowded party. Someone who talks to everyone tells you nothing
when you see them with the guest of honour — you expected that. Someone who
talks to only three people all evening, and one of them is the guest of
honour, tells you a great deal. PMI is the arithmetic of that intuition:
divide what you saw by what you had every reason to expect.
:::

```python
total = C.sum()
row = C.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
col = C.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)
with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    pmi = np.log((C * total) / (row * col))
pmi[~np.isfinite(pmi)] = 0.0
PPMI = np.maximum(pmi, 0.0)
```

```text
### PPMI for the same cells
            eats   rules   royal   sweet     the  castle
king        0.00    0.69    0.00    0.00    1.07    0.00
queen       0.00    0.59    1.06    0.00    0.67    0.00
apple       0.94    0.00    0.00    1.23    0.00    0.00
banana      0.94    0.00    0.00    1.23    0.00    0.00
```

Compare with the raw table. Among the columns shown, the `apple`–`sweet` count
is 1, half the `apple`–`eats` count; the PPMI values are nevertheless 1.23 and
0.94. The reason is the lower marginal frequency of the `sweet` context. The
transformation takes frequency into account, but it does not guarantee that an
association resting on a single observation is reliable. The highest PPMI in the
row is 2.04, for the `an` context; in this corpus `an` is followed by `apple`
every time it occurs.

::: {.column-margin}
PPMI and IDF are not the same formula, but they share an engineering
instinct: a high raw count is not information on its own. IDF measures how
rare a term is across the documents of a collection, and contributes to its
weight in a particular document once combined with TF. PMI checks whether two
words meet often only because each of them is frequent.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Intuition check: why clip the negatives instead of keeping them?

Consider two words that each occur 10 times in a million-token corpus and never
co-occur. Under independence, ignoring sentence boundaries and counting only the
tokens immediately to the left and right, the expected directed co-occurrence
count is about $2 \times 10 \times 10 / 10^6 = 0.0002$. Observing zero in this
example is unsurprising. Widening the window to two tokens on each side roughly
doubles the expectation. The PMI of a zero count goes to $-\infty$; the finite
value obtained with smoothing depends on the method chosen.

The negative PMI estimates of rare pairs can be strongly affected by sampling
uncertainty. Clipping at zero leaves those uncertain values out of the
representation and makes the matrix sparser. @levy2015improving showed that, on
the similarity and analogy benchmarks they examined, the differences between
methods mostly stayed small once hyperparameters were tuned comparably.
:::

### Step 3 — collect the repeated structure in a few dimensions

The PPMI rows already behave sensibly. (Neighbours here, and everywhere in
this chapter, are ranked by the cosine similarity of @sec-text-as-data,
$\cos(\mathbf a, \mathbf b) = \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b \,/\,
(\lVert \mathbf a \rVert\, \lVert \mathbf b \rVert)$: 1 means the two
vectors point the same way, 0 means they are orthogonal.)

```text
### nearest neighbours before factorization (PPMI rows, 19-D)
  king     queen 0.55, are 0.55, man 0.45, the 0.37
  apple    man 0.79, fruit 0.52, banana 0.40, is 0.31
  eats     a 0.55, an 0.55, man 0.34, woman 0.34
```

`king` → `queen` reflects the relationship we expected. `apple` → `man`, on the
other hand, cannot be read as synonymy. In this small corpus the two rows carry
high weights in the same columns, `an` and `eats`, and cosine measures that
overlap. `man` occurs in only one sentence of the corpus; a context overlap that
comes from a single example may not be a reliable semantic similarity.

::: {#gloss-singular-value-decomposition-svd .column-margin .term-gloss}
**singular value decomposition (SVD)** — a way of factorizing a matrix into
singular vectors and singular values. Keeping the $d$ largest singular values
and the corresponding directions gives the best rank-$d$ approximation in the
Frobenius norm. [↩](#term-singular-value-decomposition-svd){.term-back}
:::

Truncated [singular value decomposition](#gloss-singular-value-decomposition-svd){#term-singular-value-decomposition-svd .term-ref} gives you a regularisation
and compression mechanism against overlaps of that kind, which rest on a single
example. Keep only the $d$ directions with the
largest singular values and you force the model to spend its budget on the
structure that recurs, leaving one-off coincidences only whatever room is left
over. It is not a guarantee of correctness: on a small or biased corpus a
low-rank model can generalise the wrong structure too.

In this small example 19 dimensions cost nothing to compute, so compression is not
needed for speed here; the point is to watch what a low-rank representation
does to the $V$-dimensional vectors of a real system.

$$
\mathrm{PPMI} \approx U_d \Sigma_d V_d^\top, \qquad
\text{embedding} = U_d \Sigma_d
$$

We use the rows of $U_d \Sigma_d$ as each word's coordinates in this chapter.
The literature also uses $U_d$, or variants that scale the singular values by
other powers; the measured consequences of that choice come up just below.

Is that notation unfamiliar? Then here is the picture behind it.

Think of the PPMI matrix as a stack of transparencies. Each one shows a single
recurring pattern — *these words tend to sit near those words* — and each is
printed at a different darkness. Stack all 19 and you reproduce the original
matrix exactly.

The singular values in $\Sigma$ are those darknesses, sorted from boldest to
faintest. $U$ says how much each word participates in each pattern.

Truncating to $d$ means keeping only the boldest few transparencies. The
operation drops the components that belong to the small singular values; it can
reduce some accidental detail, and it can also lose useful distinctions. What is
kept is decided by the singular-value structure of the matrix, not by how many
times something repeats.

::: {.column-margin}
It can help to think of a limited storage budget: with fewer components kept,
some detail is lost. The method's criterion, however, does not line up exactly
with the detail a person finds important, or with noise.
:::

```python
d = 5
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(PPMI, full_matrices=False)
emb = U[:, :d] * S[:d]
```

In this small example we compute the full SVD and take the first five
components. For large sparse matrices a method that computes only the components
needed is preferred.

Multiplying by `S` gives more weight to the coordinates that belong to large
singular values. The scaling that minimizes reconstruction error, however, need
not be the best choice for word similarity. In the family
$W = U_d \Sigma_d^{\,p}$ the exponent $p$ can be tuned as well;
@levy2015improving show that on similarity tasks $p = 0.5$ or $p = 0$ can give
better results than $p = 1$. We use $p = 1$ here to keep the computation
visible; in practice $p$ should be chosen on validation data.

```text
### singular values (how much structure each dimension carries)
  5.75  4.76  4.03  3.71  3.64  3.08  3.03  2.80
  first 2 dimensions hold 36.8% of the sum of squares
  first 5 dimensions hold 65.4% of the sum of squares

### nearest neighbours after SVD to 5 dimensions
  king     queen 0.90, are 0.88, the 0.74, castle 0.65
  apple    banana 1.00, woman 0.86, man 0.85, fruit 0.74
  eats     an 0.95, a 0.95, man 0.64, woman 0.63
  castle   are 0.82, is 0.80, king 0.65, queen 0.61
```

Those percentages are shares of the sum of *squared* singular values. Five
components carry about two thirds of the total energy and the remaining fourteen
about one third. The ratios summarize the compression; they do not show that the
discarded components are unimportant for a task.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: what SVD "explains" is not PCA's variance

Strictly the share is of the total sum of squares $\lVert X \rVert_F^2$ and not
of variance — the PPMI matrix is never centred, so these shares are not
variance shares. (Uncentred data has a variance too; it is simply not what this
quantity measures.) The two coincide only after centring, which is what makes
the thirty-word PCA plot later in this chapter a genuinely different
calculation.
:::

The easiest way to see what happened is to put three cosines side by side,
before and after factorization:

| word pair | PPMI rows, 19-D | SVD, 5-D | what happened |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| `apple` – `banana` | 0.40 | **1.00** | never share a sentence in this corpus; the shared contexts already link them, and the compression is what makes the link decisive |
| `king` – `queen` | 0.55 | **0.90** | already right, and got stronger |
| `apple` – `man` | 0.79 | **0.85** | the one-sentence accident — *not* deleted, but no longer first |

: The same counts, compressed into five dimensions {tbl-colwidths="[24,20,16,40]"}

Look at the third row, because this step is usually described wrongly.

SVD does **not** delete the `apple`–`man` accident. That cosine *rises*, from
0.79 to 0.85. What changes is the ranking: before, `apple`'s nearest neighbour
was `man` with `banana` third; now `banana` is first and `man` third.

So the compression does not break the wrong link. It strengthens the right one
enough to overtake it — and that is what "preferring signal over noise"
actually looks like. The ordering improves; the absolute values do not.

The number to watch is the first row. `apple` and `banana` never once occur
in the same sentence in this corpus, so nothing links them *directly*. What
links them is that they keep the same company — both follow `eats`, both
precede `is sweet fruit`. The raw PPMI rows already register that as a cosine
of 0.40, because shared contexts are shared coordinates; what the compression
does is strengthen it to 1.00, enough to reorder the neighbour list. Call this
shared-context generalisation rather than transitivity — cosine similarity is
not a transitive relation in the mathematical sense — and note that low-rank
compression is what makes it decisive rather than what makes it visible.

This is latent semantic analysis [@deerwester1990indexing] applied to a
word–context matrix; the original LSA applied the same truncated SVD to a
term–document matrix, and it came before word2vec by more than twenty years.

```text
### compression
  one-hot / count row : 19 numbers per word
  svd embedding       : 5 numbers per word
    different one-hots  : cosine 0.00 (always)
  king vs queen (2-D) : cosine 0.996
  king vs banana(2-D) : cosine 0.141
```

Read 0.996 with the caveat in the box below already in mind: in a
two-dimensional space where every word shares the sign of the first
coordinate, a high cosine is partly the shared direction talking, not the
similarity.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**A detail worth noticing, because it comes back at the end of the chapter.**
In this small example the first coordinate is *negative* for every word (between
−0.70 and −2.14). That shared direction can contribute to cosine values; the
magnitudes differ, however, so the dimension is not entirely without
discriminating information. The figure below plots dimensions 2 and 3 in order
to make other distinctions visible. That choice is no substitute for the
similarities in the full space.

A space that is not spread evenly over directions is called
[anisotropic]{.hl}; a shared mean direction is one of the forms that
anisotropy can take. We will measure it on GloVe later.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Ten sentences, reduced to two coordinates — dimensions 2 and 3 of the SVD</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
toyPts = [
  {w: "king", x: -0.824, y: -0.667, g: "royalty"},
  {w: "queen", x: -1.585, y: -0.321, g: "royalty"},
```

## From counting to predicting: word2vec

So counting works. We built a space by hand, and royalty landed on one side
and food on the other. Why were prediction-based methods like word2vec taken up
so quickly?

Scalability was an important factor. A square co-occurrence matrix over 100,000
words has ten billion *possible* cells; sparse storage keeps only the non-zero
ones. In the batch PPMI–SVD pipeline used here we first accumulate the counts
and then factorize the matrix. word2vec, by contrast, learns vectors from local
training pairs without building the co-occurrence matrix explicitly. Incremental
versions of count-based methods are possible too, so this is not a distinction
that holds for every method.

::: {#gloss-word2vec .column-margin .term-gloss}
**word2vec** — a family of methods from 2013 that learn word vectors from
context. Skip-gram predicts the context words from the centre word and CBOW
predicts the centre word from the context words; the learned vectors can be
used in other tasks. [↩](#term-word2vec){.term-back}
:::

In 2013 Mikolov and colleagues published [word2vec](#gloss-word2vec){#term-word2vec .term-ref}, a method that skipped the
matrix entirely [@mikolov2013efficient; @mikolov2013distributed]. Rather than
counting co-occurrences and factorizing, train a classifier to *predict*
context — and then use the weights it learned rather than its predictions.

Architecturally, that classifier is a **shallow neural network**: an input
layer, a single hidden layer, an output layer. It is called shallow because
there is only one hidden layer. Unusually, that layer also has no activation
function — it is purely linear. In the skip-gram architecture the three layers
can be read like this:

1. The **input layer** is the centre word's one-hot vector: as long as the
   vocabulary, a single 1, zeros everywhere else.
2. The **hidden layer** multiplies that vector by a matrix $\mathbf{W}$.
   Multiplying a one-hot by a matrix selects the row belonging to that word, so
   the hidden layer is a lookup table. The selected row *is* the word's
   embedding. No further activation is applied, which is why this layer is
   often called a *projection layer* instead.
3. The **output layer** scores the selected vector against candidate context
   words. For that we use a second table, $\mathbf{W}'$, which holds one row
   per word under the full softmax and under negative sampling alike.

In CBOW the vectors of the context words are first combined: summed or
averaged.

The critical point: [the product is not the network you train, it is the
weights of the network's first layer.]{.hl} In classic word2vec use it is
mostly the input matrix $\mathbf{W}$ that is kept — one row per word, 300
numbers per row — and $\mathbf{W}'$ is set aside. That is a common choice,
not a requirement: some approaches use the output matrix, or the sum or
average of the two, and GloVe's authors recommend adding them
[@pennington2014glove]. Here we set up the prediction task in order to learn vectors
we can reuse. The input embedding table in @sec-transformers works in a similar
way; that table, however, usually has one row per token of the model's
vocabulary and not one row per word.

There are two ways to set up that prediction, and they are mirror images. Same
window, same words, arrows reversed:

| Architecture | Input | Predicts |
|---|---|---|
| **Skip-gram** | the centre word | the context words |
| **CBOW** | the context words | the centre word |

: The two word2vec architectures {tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

This chapter follows skip-gram, which is also what negative sampling is most
often paired with.

Skip-gram is the variant most analyses and tutorials use, and the rest of this
chapter follows it. (It is not the only survivor: CBOW is the default in both
the original word2vec tool and `gensim`, because it is faster.) Slide a window
over the corpus and every position yields training examples.

```{ojs}
  label: "Sentence",
```


```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sgTokens = (sgSentence || "").toLowerCase().split(/\s+/).filter(t => t.length)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sgCentre = Inputs.range([0, Math.max(0, sgTokens.length - 1)],
  {label: "Centre position", step: 1, value: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sgPairs = {
  const out = [];
  sgTokens.forEach((w, i) => {
    for (let j = Math.max(0, i - sgWindow);
         j <= Math.min(sgTokens.length - 1, i + sgWindow); j++) {
      if (i !== j) out.push({centre: w, context: sgTokens[j], ci: i, cj: j});
    }
  });
  return out;
}
```

### Negative sampling with a logistic loss {#negative-sampling-is-a-logistic-regression}


First, what exactly is skip-gram asking? Take a centre word $w$ with vector
$\mathbf{v}_w$ (its row of $\mathbf{W}$). Every candidate context word $c$ gets
a score: the dot product $\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c$ with its row of
$\mathbf{W}'$. A dot product is large when two vectors point the same way (and
are long), so
it works as a compatibility score. The original skip-gram turns these scores
into a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary with a softmax, and
training maximises the log-probability of the context words actually observed:

$$
P(c \mid w) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c)}
                   {\sum_{c'=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_{c'})},
\qquad
\text{maximise} \sum_{(w,\,c)\ \text{in the corpus}} \log P(c \mid w)
$$

For a statistician this is multinomial logistic regression with one class per
vocabulary word.

The full softmax computes and normalizes $V$ context scores for every training
pair. With $d$-dimensional vectors that costs about $O(Vd)$. When $V = 400{,}000$
(the size of the GloVe vocabulary we use later in this chapter), processing a
large number of pairs that way is expensive.

Negative sampling changes the training objective: it replaces this multi-class
task with smaller binary classification tasks. The scoring cost per pair becomes
about $O((K+1)d)$, where $K$ is the number of negative samples drawn per pair.

::: {#gloss-negative-sampling .column-margin .term-gloss}
**negative sampling** — for each observed word–context pair, drawing a small
number of contexts from a noise distribution and using them as negatively
labelled training examples. The negative examples need not be unseen in the
corpus or semantically unrelated. [↩](#term-negative-sampling){.term-back}
:::

The step that made word2vec practical replaces the 400,000-class softmax with a
question a statistician will recognise [@mikolov2013distributed]:

> Did this training example come from the distribution of observed pairs
> ($y = 1$) or from the noise sampler ($y = 0$)? The same word pair can be
> produced either way.

That is binary classification. For each observed pair $(w, c)$, draw $K$
context words from a noise distribution — a frequency-based distribution over
the vocabulary, whose exact form we return to in a few pages — and label them
0; that drawing is
the [negative sampling](#gloss-negative-sampling){#term-negative-sampling .term-ref} the method is named after. Then fit a
logistic regression whose linear predictor is the dot product of the two
words' vectors:

$$
P(y = 1 \mid w, c;\, K, q) = \sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c),
\qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}
$$

Here $q$ is the noise distribution the negative contexts are drawn from. This
probability belongs to the training sampling scheme we set up; it is not the
probability that two words occur together in the real world.


Unlike ordinary logistic regression the features are not fixed: the centre and
context vectors are learned at the same time, which makes the problem
non-convex once the two tables are considered together.

The rest is minimising the usual log loss:

$$
\mathcal{L} = -\log \sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c)
- \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \sigma(-\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_{n_k})
$$

The term for the positive pair decreases as the dot product between the centre
and context vectors grows. The term for a negative sample decreases as the
corresponding dot product shrinks. The picture of pulling together and pushing
apart describes that change in score; it does not say that the Euclidean
distance between the vectors necessarily moves the same way.

**Work one update by hand.** Vectors are 300-dimensional in practice; use 4
so the arithmetic fits on a line. Say the centre word `failed` currently has
$\mathbf{v} = (0.4,\ -0.2,\ 0.7,\ 0.1)$, its true partner `pump` has
$\mathbf{u} = (0.5,\ 0.1,\ 0.6,\ -0.3)$, and a sampled fake `opera` has
$\mathbf{u} = (-0.3,\ 0.6,\ -0.2,\ 0.4)$.

For the real pair, the dot product is

$$
(0.4)(0.5) + (-0.2)(0.1) + (0.7)(0.6) + (0.1)(-0.3) = 0.57
$$

so $\sigma(0.57) = 0.639$: under this training scheme the model gives the pair
about a 64% probability of having arrived as a positive example. The
contribution of the positively labelled example to the loss is
$-\log 0.639 = 0.448$.

For the fake pair the dot product is $-0.34$, giving $\sigma(0.34) = 0.584$
and a loss of $-\log 0.584 = 0.538$. The model is already leaning the right
way on both, but not confidently, so both will be nudged.

The update itself is where the whole thing becomes recognisable. For a single
labelled term, the derivative with respect to the dot product
$z = \mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c$ is just

$$
\ell(z, y) = -y \log \sigma(z) - (1 - y) \log\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr),
\qquad
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z} = \sigma(z) - y
$$

The derivative of the total SGNS (skip-gram with negative sampling) loss is found by adding up the derivatives of
all the positive and negative terms involved. Here $y$ is 1 for a positive
example and 0 for a negative one. **Prediction minus
target** — the same expression that falls out of every logistic regression
you have ever fitted. For `pump` that is $0.639 - 1 = -0.361$ (negative, so
the dot product goes up); for `opera` it is $0.416 - 0 = 0.416$ (positive, so
the dot product goes down).

Both vectors in a pair move. The collapsed derivation below shows the two
gradients, and each vector is dragged along the direction of the other.

To keep the arithmetic followable, let us hold the context vectors
$\mathbf{u}$ fixed and update only the centre vector $\mathbf{v}$. Its
gradient is the *sum* of both terms — that is what the loss above says, and
what `gv` in the training code below computes in one `einsum`:

$$
g_{\mathbf v} = (0.639 - 1)\,\mathbf u_{\texttt{pump}}
              + (0.416 - 0)\,\mathbf u_{\texttt{opera}}
              = (-0.305,\ 0.213,\ -0.300,\ 0.275)
$$

With a learning rate of 0.05 that moves `failed`·`pump` from 0.570 to **0.590**
and `failed`·`opera` from $-0.340$ to $-0.359$.

Update the context vectors too, as a real implementation does, and the same
step lands on **0.603** and $-0.374$ — the same directions, moved roughly 1.7
times as far.

Those are tiny movements. Multiply them by tens of billions of pairs and you
get the geometry that made these models famous. Do not draw the wrong
conclusion from that: the mathematics of a single SGD update is surprisingly
simple, but "word2vec is plain SGD and the rest does not matter" is not true.
[Much of what decides the quality is not in the update itself but in which
pairs are shown, how often, and against what]{.hl} — the sampling and
training strategies: negative sampling, subsampling of frequent words, the
noise distribution and the context window. A few pages on we take those four
one at a time.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The gradient in full, for the reader who wants to see it fall out

Take the real-pair term alone, and write $z = \mathbf{v}_w \cdot
\mathbf{u}_c$. The single fact you need is that the sigmoid has an
unusually tidy derivative:

$$
\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\,\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr)
$$

Now differentiate $-\log \sigma(z)$ with the chain rule:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\bigl[-\log \sigma(z)\bigr]
= -\frac{\sigma'(z)}{\sigma(z)}
= -\frac{\sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))}{\sigma(z)}
= \sigma(z) - 1
$$

The $\sigma(z)$ cancels. That is a pleasant property, but it is not the
*main* reason log loss is paired with the sigmoid; the main reason is about
probability, and it is worth seeing step by step.

The label of every training example is 0 or 1. The probability distribution
describing a single trial with a yes/no outcome is called the **Bernoulli
distribution**; a coin flip is an example. We model the label with it. Its
parameter $p$ lies in the interval $[0, 1]$. Our model supplies that $p$: for
finite $z$ the sigmoid produces $p = \sigma(z)$ in the interval $(0, 1)$.

Now ask: how much probability did the model give to the answer we actually
observed? If the answer was "yes" ($y = 1$) that probability is $p$; if it was
"no" ($y = 0$) it is $1 - p$. This number is called the **likelihood**: how
probable the model considered what in fact happened. A good model gives high
probability to what happened, so the natural target of training is to make the
likelihood large. Adding logarithms is easier than multiplying those
probabilities across all pairs, and a minus sign turns "make large" into "make
small":

$$
-\log(\text{likelihood}) \;=\; -\bigl[\,y \log p + (1 - y)\log(1 - p)\,\bigr]
$$

That expression is **binary cross-entropy**: the negative log-likelihood of the
Bernoulli model. Making it small makes the likelihood of the observed labels
large. Probability estimates can also be evaluated with a squared loss; that is
a different criterion, however, and not the same as the Bernoulli log loss
derived here.

In short, pairing the sigmoid with log loss buys two things at once: a clean
probabilistic reading through the Bernoulli likelihood *and* a gradient as
simple as the one above. The second is a gift of the first. For a negative
sample the term
is $-\log \sigma(-z)$ and the same two lines give $\sigma(z)$. Both cases
collapse into $\sigma(z) - y$.

Getting from there to the vectors is one more chain-rule step, because
$\partial z / \partial \mathbf{v}_w = \mathbf{u}_c$:

$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{v}_w}
= \bigl(\sigma(z) - y\bigr)\, \mathbf{u}_c,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{u}_c}
= \bigl(\sigma(z) - y\bigr)\, \mathbf{v}_w
$$

The gradient of each vector is the scalar error $\sigma(z) - y$ multiplied by the
other vector. When the model gives the correct label a high probability, the
scalar error becomes small. Vector norms can grow, however, and the
contributions within a batch can add up, so this property alone does not
guarantee stable training or convergence. The learning rate, the gradient scale
and, where needed, clipping have to be considered separately.
:::

::::

The sigmoid and the log loss that SGNS uses
for each labelled pair are familiar from logistic regression. But the vectors on
both sides of the dot product are learned as well, so the model as a whole is
not classical logistic regression with fixed features. A more accurate
description is logistic matrix factorization, in which two vector tables are
learned together. That distinction explains both the familiar form of the
gradients and the non-convexity of the joint optimization.

::: {.column-margin}
Two matrices are learned, not one: $\mathbf{v}_w$ for words as centres and
$\mathbf{u}_c$ for words as contexts. Almost everyone discards $\mathbf{u}$
and keeps $\mathbf{v}$. Adding them sometimes helps a little; GloVe's
authors recommend it [@pennington2014glove].
:::

:::

### Which vectors get updated in one step?

To understand the computational cost of negative sampling, look at which rows a
single training pair contributes to.

For a single training pair, with $K = 5$ negatives, there are **seven row
updates** across the two matrices:

- **one** row of $\mathbf{W}$: the centre word's vector $\mathbf{v}_w$.
- **one** row of $\mathbf{W}'$: the true context word's vector
  $\mathbf{u}_c$.
- **$K$** rows of $\mathbf{W}'$: the vectors of the sampled fake words.

If the sampled negatives repeat, or collide with the true context word, the
number of *distinct* rows touched is fewer than seven; the number of update
contributions does not change.

The remaining rows — those of every other word in the vocabulary, in both
matrices — do not enter the SGNS data loss of this pair, so their gradients are
*zero*. Under the SGD update used here, which has no momentum and no weight
decay, those rows do not change. With regularization, or with an optimizer that
carries past updates forward, the parameter update has to be examined
separately.

For scale, take the model we train from scratch below: two tables of 18,677
words and 100 dimensions hold 37,354 rows and 3,735,400 parameters in total. A
single training pair with five negatives contributes to **at most seven
distinct rows**, about **0.019%** of them. That sparsity is one of the important
reasons training is efficient.

You can see it directly in the update lines of the code below: `targets` in
`np.add.at(Wo, targets.ravel(), ...)` holds only $K+1$ indices per pair, so
only that many rows of `Wo` are added into. The rest are untouched.

**With a full softmax** every output vector takes part in the scoring in the
denominator and usually receives a non-zero gradient. In this example that is
one centre row and 18,677 output rows, 18,678 rows in total. The ratio of about
**2,668** against seven rows compares the number of rows affected; it is not a
ratio of total computational cost or of running time.

::: {.column-margin}
In SGNS the table is accessed only through the selected indices, so the gradient
of the data loss is **sparse** at the level of rows. PyTorch's
`nn.Embedding(..., sparse=True)` produces sparse gradients for accesses of this
kind. If the embedding parameters are also used in other operations, such as a
full softmax, the gradient of the whole parameter need not be sparse. Here the
centre vector is updated directly when the word is selected as a centre, and
the context vector when it is used as a positive or a negative context.
:::

### Four training choices that decide how well word2vec works

The update itself was simple. *How good* the model is depends largely on the
four choices below; each one answers part of the question "which pairs do we
show, how often, and against what?"

| choice | what it sets | typical value | effect |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Number of negatives** ($K$) | negatives drawn per positive pair | 5–20 for a small corpus and 2–5 for a large one in the original work | changes the balance between cost and training signal |
| **Context window** | candidate neighbours and weighting by distance | for example at most 5, with the dynamic-window option | narrow windows can bring out functional relations more, wide ones topical relations |
| **Subsampling frequent words** ($t$) | probability of keeping very frequent tokens | for example $t = 10^{-3}$ | reduces the share of frequent words in training |
| **Noise distribution** (the 0.75 exponent) | probability of drawing each negative | $q(w) \propto f(w)^{0.75}$ | raises the relative sampling share of rare words compared with the raw unigram distribution |

: word2vec's four training choices {tbl-colwidths="[24,30,22,24]"}

**Negative sampling and $K$.** You have seen the method itself: for each real
pair, $K$ fake context words are drawn from a noise distribution and the model
learns to tell real from fake. What is tuned here is $K$. With a very small
$K$ the model sees too few "not this one" examples and the vectors do not
separate enough; a large $K$ makes every step more expensive. The original
paper suggests 5–20 for small corpora and 2–5 for large ones
[@mikolov2013distributed] — with plenty of data every word already gets many
updates, so a few negatives are enough.

**The context window.** With a window of 5, up to five tokens to the left and up
to five to the right of the centre, within the same input sequence, are
candidate contexts. Narrow windows (1–2) mostly reflect close syntactic
relations, and wide windows (5–10) reflect topical relations more. Those are
tendencies; the corpus, the language and the preprocessing affect the outcome
too. If sentence boundaries are kept, the window does not cross them.

word2vec adds one more refinement: it does not keep the window fixed. For each
centre word it draws the effective width at random between 1 and the maximum
(a dynamic window). The result is that near neighbours produce training pairs
more often than distant ones — an implicit weighting by distance. You can
change the window by hand in the counting method at the start of the chapter
and see the difference yourself (exercise 1).

**Subsampling frequent words.** Frequent words produce a large number of
training pairs. To reduce their relative influence, each token is kept with a
probability that depends on its frequency. Below, $f(w)$ is the relative
frequency among the tokens left after the vocabulary filter, and $t$ is a
threshold on the same scale. The keep probability used is

$$
p_{\text{keep}}(w) = \min\!\left(1,\ \left(\sqrt{\frac{f(w)}{t}} + 1\right)\cdot\frac{t}{f(w)}\right),
\qquad t \approx 10^{-3}
$$

The formula looks arbitrary until you put numbers through it. The threshold
$t = 10^{-3}$ sets the scale: any word making up less than a thousandth of the
corpus comes out with the inner expression above 1 and is simply always kept,
which is what the $\min$ is doing. (The exact break-even point is a little
higher, at $f \approx 2.6\,t$ — about 0.26% of the corpus — where the inner
expression equals exactly 1.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: the formula in the paper and the formula in the code

The original C implementation uses the keep formula above. The paper gives
$P(\text{discard}) = 1 - \sqrt{t/f}$; that expression is negative when
$f < t$, so as a probability it is read as
$P(\text{discard}) = \max(0,\ 1 - \sqrt{t/f})$, that is
$P(\text{keep}) = \min(1,\ \sqrt{t/f})$. The two formulas are not the same;
when reproducing an experiment, state which implementation was used.
:::

| share of corpus | example | $p_{\text{keep}}$ | discarded |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| 5% | `the` in English text | 0.16 | 84% |
| 1% | `of`, `and` | 0.42 | 58% |
| 0.1% ($=t$) | mid-frequency word | 1.00 | 0% |
| 0.01% and below | everything in the tail | 1.00 | 0% |

: What subsampling actually throws away {tbl-colwidths="[22,30,24,24]"}

So this is not a gentle reweighting. It deletes five out of every six
occurrences of `the`, and it does not touch the tail at all — rare words are
left alone while the top of the Zipf curve you plotted in @sec-text-as-data
is aggressively thinned.

In the run below it discards 26.6% of the in-vocabulary tokens: 6,397,826
become 4,698,743. Almost all of what it throws away is `the`, `of`, `and` and
their friends.

(Where does 6,397,826 come from? It is what is left of the run's
`tokens read: 6794527` once everything below `min_count=20` is dropped. The
subsampling rate applies to that.)

::: {.column-margin}
When a token is removed, the words on either side of it move closer together in
the remaining sequence. The window size does not change, but words that were
further apart in the original text can now form new context pairs. That changes
both the number of training examples and the context distribution.
:::

**The noise distribution: the 0.75 exponent.** The *noise distribution* is
the name for the distribution the fake context words are drawn from. Negative samples are not drawn from the unigram
distribution but from $P(w) \propto f(w)^{0.75}$. Raising every probability to
a power below 1 pulls all of them toward 1, and it pulls the smallest ones
furthest in relative terms: $0.5^{0.75}$ is 19% larger than $0.5$, while
$0.001^{0.75}$ is 5.6 times larger than $0.001$. Renormalising afterwards
therefore moves probability mass out of the head of the distribution and into
the tail.

Concretely: if a common word is 5,000 times more frequent than a rare one,
then after the exponent it is only $5000^{0.75} \approx 595$ times more
likely to be drawn as a negative. The gap narrows by a factor of about eight,
and it narrows in the rare word's favour.

Negative samples make the context vectors receive updates from pairs drawn from
the noise distribution as well as from the observed positive pairs. The 0.75
exponent raises the relative share of rare contexts compared with raw unigram
sampling; it does not give them a kind of signal that did not exist before. The
centre vectors are affected indirectly too, through those changing context
vectors. The exponent also changes the noise distribution in the implicit
objective of SGNS; a later Deep dive box examines that connection. 0.75 is an
empirical choice, not a universal theoretical optimum. @levy2015improving show
that hyperparameters of this kind can affect comparison results substantially.

### Deep dive: writing word2vec from scratch

For the main storyline, the training loop is six steps:

1. take a real (centre, context) pair from the corpus;
2. draw $K$ fake context words from the noise distribution;
3. compute the dot products between the centre vector and those $K+1$ vectors;
4. apply the sigmoid;
5. take the error, prediction minus label;
6. update the corresponding rows of the two tables with that error.

The NumPy example below shows the training pipeline used with the first 40
million characters of the `text8` corpus (a cleaned dump of English Wikipedia).
The data preparation and the update steps are visible; the lines that report
the loss, the time and the neighbours printed underneath are not part of this
abridged listing (the full code is in the chapter notebook). The basic gradient
comes from the logistic loss above; the gradient clipping below changes the
update rule. If the numerical details — batching, sampling, gradient clipping —
are not what you are here for, skip to the results.

```python
import gzip, time
from collections import Counter
import numpy as np
import gensim.downloader as api

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

with gzip.open(api.load("text8", return_path=True), "rt") as f:
    raw = f.read(40_000_000).split()

MIN_COUNT = 20
counts = Counter(raw)
vocab = [w for w, c in counts.most_common() if c >= MIN_COUNT]
idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
V = len(vocab)

total = sum(counts[w] for w in vocab)
freq = np.array([counts[w] / total for w in vocab])
keep = np.minimum(1.0, (np.sqrt(freq / 1e-3) + 1) * (1e-3 / freq))

ids = np.array([idx[w] for w in raw if w in idx], dtype=np.int32)
ids = ids[rng.random(len(ids)) < keep[ids]]          # subsampling

noise = freq ** 0.75                                  # the 0.75 exponent
noise /= noise.sum()
cum = np.cumsum(noise)

D, K, WINDOW, EPOCHS, LR0 = 100, 5, 5, 3, 0.02
Wc = ((rng.random((V, D)) - 0.5) / D).astype(np.float32)   # centre vectors
Wo = np.zeros((V, D), dtype=np.float32)                    # context vectors

# Two simplifications. (1) The window is fixed at 5; no dynamic window is used.
# (2) text8 is processed as a single token stream. The original sentence and
# document boundaries are not kept, so artificial context pairs can form
# across them. With separate documents, build the pairs within each document.
centres, contexts = [], []
for off in range(1, WINDOW + 1):
    centres.append(ids[:-off]); contexts.append(ids[off:])
    centres.append(ids[off:]); contexts.append(ids[:-off])
centres = np.concatenate(centres)
contexts = np.concatenate(contexts)
N = len(centres)

BATCH = 2048
n_batches = N // BATCH

def sigmoid(x):
    # Overflow-safe sigmoid; it does not artificially restrict the score to [-8, 8].
    return np.exp(-np.logaddexp(0.0, -x))

for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    for b in range(n_batches):
        # drawn WITH replacement: "3 epochs" means three times as many
        # pair-draws as there are pairs, not three passes. About 5% of pairs
        # are never drawn and some are drawn six times, so do not compare
        # EPOCHS=3 here with epochs=3 in gensim.
        sl = rng.integers(0, N, BATCH)
        c, o = centres[sl], contexts[sl]
        negs = np.searchsorted(cum, rng.random((BATCH, K))).astype(np.int32)
        targets = np.concatenate([o[:, None], negs], axis=1)   # (B, K+1)
        labels = np.zeros((BATCH, K + 1), dtype=np.float32)
        labels[:, 0] = 1.0                       # first column is the real pair

        v = Wc[c]                                              # (B, D)
        u = Wo[targets]                                        # (B, K+1, D)
        score = sigmoid(np.einsum("bkd,bd->bk", u, v))         # (B, K+1)
        err = (score - labels).astype(np.float32)              # the negated residual

        lr = LR0 * max(1e-4, 1 - (epoch * n_batches + b) / (EPOCHS * n_batches))
        gv = np.einsum("bk,bkd->bd", err, u)
        gu = err[:, :, None] * v[:, None, :]
        np.clip(gv, -1.0, 1.0, out=gv)
        np.clip(gu, -1.0, 1.0, out=gu)
        np.add.at(Wc, c, -lr * gv)
        np.add.at(Wo, targets.ravel(), (-lr * gu).reshape(-1, D))

E = Wc / (np.linalg.norm(Wc, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)
```

Look at the line `err = score - labels`. That is *predicted minus observed* —
the residual of a logistic regression (observed minus predicted) with its sign
flipped, which is the form the log-loss gradient uses directly. Every gradient
below it is that difference times the other vector. If the statistics feels familiar, it should.

```text

vocabulary (min_count=20): 18677
tokens after subsampling: 4698743
training pairs: 46987400
### training

    epoch 1  100.0%  loss  2.409
```

The loss at the end of each epoch is the mean over that epoch's last 1,000
batches; the time depends on the machine.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Intuition check: why does `np.add.at` need gradient clipping here?

Real word2vec updates one pair at a time, so a frequent word's vector is
refreshed between updates. Batching breaks that: `np.add.at` *accumulates*
every gradient for a repeated index and applies the sum in one step. In a
batch of 2048 pairs, a common word can appear a hundred times, so it
receives a hundred stacked updates computed from a vector that never moved.

Without clipping this run diverges to `nan` within half an epoch — which is
exactly what happened the first time it was run for this chapter, at learning
rate 0.05.

Here the clip is applied before the contributions of repeated indices are summed.
The total gradient of the centre example and the gradient of each context
example are restricted to $[-1, 1]$ per coordinate. If a row receives a hundred
contributions, each of its coordinates can change by at most
$100 \times \text{lr}$, and its L2 norm in $d$ dimensions by at most
$100 \times \text{lr} \times \sqrt{d}$. The operation bounds individual
contributions; it does not directly bound the accumulated row update.

One option is to divide the gradient of the whole batch by the batch size and
choose the learning rate accordingly. Another is to divide each row's
accumulated gradient by the number of contributions its index has in the batch;
`np.bincount` can compute those counts. The second option scales the effective
learning rates of the rows differently and is not the same as the standard batch
mean. Neither reproduces sequential SGD, which updates the parameters again at
every example.

Gradient clipping is an optimization choice made in this implementation, and it
can affect the vectors that are learned. Vectorization does not necessarily
require clipping; the scaling of the batch loss, the learning rate and the
update scheme have to be tuned together. The divergence reported in this example
belongs to the run made with the settings chosen.
:::

### The link between count-based and prediction-based methods {#the-two-families-were-one-family-all-along}


For a while counting (LSA, PPMI+SVD) and predicting (word2vec) were seen as rival
approaches; @baroni2014dont compared the two and reported better results for
prediction-based methods. Then @levy2014neural showed how skip-gram with
negative sampling relates to matrix factorization. If the negative contexts are
drawn from the context marginal of the training pairs, and if the dot product
of every pair can be chosen independently, then for pairs with a positive count
the optimal target is the shifted **PMI** value below. That does not mean every
version of word2vec is identical to PPMI–SVD:

$$
\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c = \mathrm{PMI}(w, c) - \log K
$$

So prediction-based SGNS and matrix-based methods are closer than they looked:
under those conditions the optimal dot products target a shifted PMI. The
low-rank constraint, different losses and sampling mean they still do not
produce the same embedding in practice.

Note that this is PMI, not the PPMI of route A. When building an explicit matrix
we can clip the PMI values that are negative or go to infinity and obtain the
*shifted positive* PMI that Levy and Goldberg propose,
$\mathrm{SPPMI}(w,c) = \max(\mathrm{PMI}(w,c) - \log K,\ 0)$. SGNS does not do
that explicitly. A pair whose positive count is zero can still be drawn as a
negative; with $q(c) > 0$ and a positive centre probability, the logistic
optimum for its free score lies at the limit $z \to -\infty$. The actual model
works with finite parameters, shared low-dimensional vectors and a finite number
of updates, so it does not realize all those limits exactly.

SGNS does not build this matrix explicitly; it makes updates from sampled pairs.
Shared low-dimensional vectors may not be able to meet the free optima of all
pairs at once. The noise distribution with the 0.75 exponent changes the target
as well. For those reasons not every dot product of a converged implementation
equals $\mathrm{PMI} - \log K$ directly.

When $K$ grows, with the other distributions held fixed, the free dot-product
targets shift down by the same constant. That is not in general equivalent to
adding the same vector to every word vector. Adding a constant to the target
matrix raises its rank by at most one; it can be represented with an extra
coordinate if needed, but the same fit may not be preserved at a fixed $d$. The
effect of $K$ on a task has to be assessed experimentally.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: why SGNS learns a shifted PMI

Fix a single pair $(w, c)$ and treat $z = \mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c$ as a
free number, not as something built from vectors. Over the whole corpus that
pair contributes two terms to the objective: one proportional to its positive
count, and one proportional to how often the sampler would produce it as a
negative. Assuming the negatives are drawn from the context marginal $P(c)$,
those two weights are $P(w,c)$ and $K \cdot P(w)P(c)$. The pair's contribution
to the objective **to be maximized** is the following; taking the negative of
the same expression gives the loss to be minimized:

$$
P(w,c)\,\log \sigma(z) \;+\; K\,P(w)P(c)\,\log \sigma(-z)
$$

Differentiate with respect to $z$, using $\frac{d}{dz}\log\sigma(z) = 1 -
\sigma(z)$ and $\frac{d}{dz}\log\sigma(-z) = -\sigma(z)$, and set the result
to zero:

$$
P(w,c)\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr) = K\,P(w)P(c)\,\sigma(z)
$$

Solve for $\sigma(z)$, then convert back through $z = \log
\frac{\sigma(z)}{1-\sigma(z)}$:

$$
z = \log \frac{P(w,c)}{K\,P(w)P(c)}
  = \log \frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)P(c)} - \log K
  = \mathrm{PMI}(w,c) - \log K
$$

This derivation assumes that the negatives are drawn from $P(c)$ and that $z$
can be chosen independently for every pair. In the actual low-dimensional model
all the dot products are built from shared vectors. Under that constraint SGNS
optimizes a logistic loss weighted by sampling. PPMI–SVD, by contrast,
minimizes the squared reconstruction error of a matrix whose negative values
have been clipped. So the two can differ in their targets as well as in their
losses, because of the clipping and the noise distribution.

The assumption that negatives are drawn from $P(c)$, the *raw* unigram
distribution, does not match the code above. word2vec draws them from
$P_\alpha(c) \propto f(c)^{0.75}$ instead — the exponent from two sections
ago — and carrying that through gives

$$
\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c
  = \log \frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)\,P_\alpha(c)} - \log K
$$

which is PMI computed against a *smoothed* context distribution.
@levy2015improving call this context distribution smoothing, and show it
transfers straight to PPMI+SVD, where it is worth several points. So the 0.75
exponent is not a sampling detail bolted onto the algorithm: it changes which
matrix the algorithm factorizes.
:::

figure additionally clips at zero and uses a squared loss; it is not expected to

distribution $q(c)$ has to replace $P(c)$ in the equality under the figure.

::::

@levy2015improving followed up by showing that once you give the
count-based methods the same hyperparameters word2vec quietly uses —
subsampling, context distribution smoothing, dynamic windows — the
performance gap mostly disappears.

The lesson generalises well beyond embeddings, and it is worth carrying into
every paper you read: when a new method beats an old one, some of the
improvement is the method and some is the tuning, and the split is rarely
reported.

Which leaves the practical question of when to take which route. Since their
targets are close and they land close enough that @levy2015improving could not
separate them once the hyperparameters matched, the choice is mostly about
engineering:

| | [Counting]{.pro} (PPMI + SVD) | [Predicting]{.pro} (word2vec) |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Large corpora need a sparse co-occurrence matrix, the low-rank vectors and the solver's working memory. The small example in this chapter uses a dense matrix for teaching purposes | In a streaming implementation the two vector tables take $O(Vd)$ space; the sampler and buffers need memory too. The NumPy example here stores every pair, so its total memory also depends on corpus size |
| Corpus size | Comfortable on small corpora, where every count is precious | Needs a lot of text before the gradient noise averages out |
| Reproducibility | The solver and the environment are fixed; randomized SVD needs a stated seed. The signs of singular vectors, and some choices of basis in subspaces with equal singular values, are not unique | Controlling the seed, data order, thread count and environment improves reproducibility; different initializations can give different solutions |
| New data | Counts can be updated incrementally; the reweighting and the factorization need a suitable update method | Training can continue if the two tables, the vocabulary and the necessary training state have been kept. Released word vectors alone may not be enough |
| Inspectability | Counts and weighted cells can be inspected directly | The sampling distribution, gradients, norms, loss and neighbourhoods can be inspected |
| Tuning burden | Window size, PPMI variant, $d$ | Window, $d$, $K$, subsampling $t$, learning rate, epochs |

: Close targets, different engineering {tbl-colwidths="[19,40,41]"}

One more difference does not fit in that table, and it is statistical. Truncated
SVD gives the best rank-$d$ approximation in Frobenius norm (the
Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem), which means it gives an equal coefficient to the
squared reconstruction error of every cell of the PPMI matrix. The zeros in
PPMI cover pairs that were never observed and also observed pairs whose PMI is
zero or negative. The sheer number of zeros does not by itself show that most of
the error, or of the model's capacity, goes to them. SGNS uses a logistic loss
under weights set by the positive pair frequencies and the negative-sampling
distribution. GloVe chooses yet another weighting, one that depends on the
counts, as the next section shows. Those differences affect how the methods
behave; they do not prove an unconditional advantage for any of them on rare
words.

The choice should weigh corpus size, the need for updates, memory,
inspectability and the target task together. PPMI–SVD makes the steps of the
computation visible on small examples; streaming SGNS can be convenient for
training on large text that keeps arriving. How well either approach does
depends on the implementation and the settings used.

## GloVe: counting, with a loss function

GloVe accumulates the co-occurrence counts explicitly and learns the vectors
with a weighted loss function defined on those counts. In that way it combines
a count-based representation with gradient-based learning.

GloVe's input is a word–context co-occurrence table. The matrix $C$ at the start
of the chapter added one for every pair inside the window. In the original
GloVe implementation distant contexts can be counted with a lower weight, so
the cells of $X$ need not be integers. Both approaches accumulate information
from local windows across the corpus.

GloVe learns vectors and bias terms for every word and every context. It asks
the sum $\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c + b_w + b_c$ to be close to the
logarithm of the positive co-occurrence count. Closeness is measured by the
squared error multiplied by a weight that depends on the pair's count: weighted
**least squares**. Because the two vector tables are learned together, this is
not the same optimization problem, in its parameters, as ordinary linear
regression.

More formally: [GloVe factorizes co-occurrence counts accumulated from local
windows across the whole corpus, using a weighted least-squares
objective.]{.hl}

The "accumulated from local windows" part matters, because it corrects a
common wrong intuition. It is true that GloVe uses "global statistics", but
the global table does not come from nowhere: it is built from the same local
context windows word2vec sees, added up over the entire corpus. The difference
is not whether windows are used but *when* the learning happens: word2vec sees
context examples one at a time and makes an update from each; GloVe counts and
totals them all first, then optimises against the totals. The original paper
presents the method as a combination of the two: bringing together the
advantages of global matrix factorization and local context-window methods
[@pennington2014glove].

Putting the three methods side by side: PPMI+SVD transforms the whole
co-occurrence table first and factorizes it afterwards. word2vec does an
implicit factorization through local training pairs. GloVe keeps the counts
gathered from the windows explicitly and optimises low-dimensional vectors to
account for those counts directly.

GloVe [@pennington2014glove] took that synthesis seriously. Build the global
co-occurrence matrix, then fit vectors so that dot products reproduce log
co-occurrence counts, weighting rare pairs down:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \sum_{(w,c)\,:\,X_{wc} > 0} f(X_{wc})
\left(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c + b_w + b_c - \log X_{wc}\right)^2
$$

This is weighted least squares on log counts, with a bias term per word —
about as classical as statistics gets. Take it apart piece by piece, because
every term is there for a reason.

**Why $\log X_{wc}$ and not $X_{wc}$?** Co-occurrence counts can span a very
wide range: some pairs are frequent and a great many are rare. A squared error
on raw counts can give the pairs with large counts far too much prominence. The
logarithm turns multiplicative ratios into additive differences and reduces
that difference in scale.

**Why the bias terms?** The bias terms can model part of the overall usage
tendencies of the word and of the context. That carries an intuition similar to
the way PMI takes marginal frequencies into account. GloVe learns these terms
jointly from the data, however, and they need not equal the log row and column
totals. So GloVe's dot products cannot be read as exactly PMI.

**Why $f(X_{wc})$?** Two problems need solving at once. A pair that never
co-occurs has $\log 0 = -\infty$, and a pair that co-occurs constantly would
swamp everything else. GloVe's weighting function handles both:

$$
f(x) = \begin{cases}
(x / x_{\max})^{3/4} & x < x_{\max} \\
1 & x \geq x_{\max}
\end{cases}
\qquad x_{\max} = 100
$$

| $X_{wc}$ | $f(X_{wc})$ | effect on that pair |
|--:|--:|---|
| 0 | 0.00 | never enters the objective — no $\log 0$ problem |
| 1 | 0.03 | counted, but barely |
| 10 | 0.18 | growing weight |
| 100 | 1.00 | full weight |
| 100,000 | 1.00 | *also* full weight — the cap has bitten |

: GloVe's weighting function, at $x_{\max} = 100$ {tbl-colwidths="[16,18,66]"}

Because cells with a zero count are left out of the sum, $\log 0$ is never
computed. For positive counts $f(x)$ lowers the weight of rare pairs and stays
at 1 for $x \geq 100$. The weight therefore does not grow without bound as the
count grows; the squared residual and the gradient can still be large. In its
aim of controlling the influence of frequent pairs this is related to
subsampling; it is not the same operation. The 0.75 exponent that appears in
both methods does different jobs as well.

For the rest of the chapter we use GloVe's pretrained vectors as an easily
obtained example of a static representation.

```python
import numpy as np
import gensim.downloader as api

g = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-100")   # Wikipedia 2014 + Gigaword 5, 6 billion tokens
print("vectors:", len(g.index_to_key), " dimensions:", g.vector_size)
v = g["king"]
print("king[:8] =", np.round(v[:8], 3))
print("norm:", round(float(np.linalg.norm(v)), 3))
```

```text
vectors: 400000  dimensions: 100
king[:8] = [-0.323 -0.876  0.22   0.253  0.23   0.739 -0.38  -0.353]
norm: 6.118
```

Every word is now represented by one hundred numbers. No labels such as
"royalty" or "gender" were assigned to these coordinates in advance. Some
coordinates may turn out to be related to particular properties; such readings
depend on the chosen representation, however, and are usually not preserved
when the coordinate system changes.

```python
for w in ["king", "pump", "turkey", "python", "bank"]:
    print(f"  {w:<8} " + ", ".join(f"{a} {b:.2f}"
          for a, b in g.most_similar(w, topn=6)))
```

```text
  king     prince 0.77, queen 0.75, son 0.70, brother 0.70, monarch 0.70, throne 0.69
  pump     pumps 0.84, pumping 0.77, pumped 0.71, gasoline 0.64, fuel 0.63, petrol 0.63
  turkey   ankara 0.75, turkish 0.72, greece 0.71, syria 0.70, bulgaria 0.69, russia 0.69
  python   monty 0.69, php 0.59, perl 0.58, cleese 0.54, flipper 0.51, ruby 0.51
  bank     banks 0.81, banking 0.75, credit 0.70, investment 0.69, financial 0.68, securities 0.67
```

Three of these deserve a second look.

Among the neighbours of `turkey` the words about the country stand out, and
among those of `bank` the words about finance. For `python`, neighbours related
to the comedy troupe (`monty`, `cleese`) and to programming languages (`php`,
`perl`) appear together. Which usage relations the `flipper` result comes from
cannot be determined from this list alone. The lists show that a single word
vector can carry the influence of different usages together; they are not a
complete inventory of all the senses.

This is the defining limitation of a static embedding: [one vector per word
form, whatever the context]{.hl}.

The Turkish word *yüz* can mean *face*, the number *hundred*, or the imperative
*swim*. A static word table gives that form a single vector; the different
usages influence what is learned, but the result is not an explicitly computed
arithmetic mean of those senses. Querying the vector by itself cannot select
which sense is in use in the sentence at hand. A model that processes this
vector together with the surrounding words, on the other hand, can make use of
the context.

That limitation is one of the important reasons for the token representations
that change with context, covered in @sec-transformers.

## Word analogies and the conditions of evaluation {#the-famous-analogy-and-what-it-hides}

With the `king − man + woman` example we look at what vector arithmetic shows
and at how the result depends on choices made in the computation.

The result that made embeddings famous outside NLP:

```python
res = g.most_similar(positive=["king", "woman"], negative=["man"], topn=5)
```

```text
  queen        0.7699
  monarch      0.6843
  throne       0.6756
  daughter     0.6595
  princess     0.6521
```

$\text{king} - \text{man} + \text{woman} \approx \text{queen}$. Among the
candidates allowed, `queen` is the word with the highest cosine similarity to
the target this operation builds. The result indicates that some relations can
be represented by similar vector differences. An exact parallelogram is
sufficient for the arithmetic to produce the `queen` vector itself; it is not
necessary for `queen` to be selected as the nearest neighbour. Nor can we
conclude from this example that the differences between `man` and `woman`, and
between `king` and `queen`, consist of a single gender direction only.

`gensim.most_similar` normalizes each input vector to unit length separately
and removes the input words from the candidates. To see the effect of the
filter alone, rank the same scores with two candidate sets; `topn=None` returns
the unfiltered scores for the whole vocabulary:

```python
sims = g.most_similar(positive=["king", "woman"], negative=["man"], topn=None)
inputs = {"king", "man", "woman"}
order = np.argsort(-sims)
for label, excluded in [("unfiltered", set()), ("filtered", inputs)]:
    chosen = [i for i in order if g.index_to_key[i] not in excluded][:6]
    print(label)
    for i in chosen:
        print(f"  {g.index_to_key[i]:<12} {sims[i]:.4f}")
```

```text
unfiltered
  king         0.8361
  queen        0.7699
  monarch      0.6843
  throne       0.6756
  daughter     0.6595
  princess     0.6521
filtered
  queen        0.7699
  monarch      0.6843
  throne       0.6756
  daughter     0.6595
  princess     0.6521
  prince       0.6517
```

With the scores held fixed, the unfiltered nearest neighbour is **`king`**
(0.8361) and `queen` is second (0.7699). That is the result of an unrestricted
neighbour search; it does not show that the expected answer to the analogy is
`king`. Excluding the input words defines a different candidate set, and in
that set `queen` comes first. The candidate set is part of the definition of
the task and has to be stated with the result. If the inputs are added without
normalizing them first, the scores change a little (`king` 0.8552, `queen`
0.7834); the top of the ranking stays the same.

This scoring is called **3CosAdd**: it combines the candidate's cosines with
the three inputs using two plus signs and one minus sign. Excluding the input
words is a separate evaluation rule. **3CosMul** shifts the cosines suitably
and combines them as a multiplicative ratio; it gives better results in some
evaluations [@levy2014linguistic]. The scoring method and the candidate filter
should be reported separately.

The deeper objection is @linzen2016issues'. He shows that a baseline which
ignores the relation entirely — return the nearest neighbour of `king`, never
look at `man` or `woman` — already recovers a large share of the reported
accuracy on some categories. On this example it would be wrong — `king`'s
nearest neighbour is `prince` (0.77) — but the GloVe neighbour list above shows
how much of the work the structure has already done: `queen` is already
`king`'s second-nearest neighbour (0.75) before any arithmetic, so the offset
only has to move it up one place, and in some categories the nearest neighbour
is already the answer. So the headline number measures neighbourhood structure at least as
much as it measures a relation. @nissim2020fair show that excluding the input
words can also affect how bias analogies are read. In the examples they examine,
`doctor` can become a candidate again once the filter is removed; the model, the
normalization and the candidate set a result was obtained with should be stated
together. Try a few for yourself:

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Analogy explorer — real GloVe results, with and without the filter</div>
```
