```{ojs}
that carry the most variance of these thirty points, and because the points
already come from five distinct clusters, the between-cluster differences land
on those directions. They keep only <b>37.5%</b> of the variance of
```

## fastText: words made of pieces

Everything so far shares one assumption we have not questioned: that a word
is an indivisible unit with its own row in a table. Which raises a question
you already know the answer to if you read @sec-text-as-data — what happens
when a word is not in the table?

::: {#gloss-out-of-vocabulary-oov .column-margin .term-gloss}
**out-of-vocabulary (OOV)** — a form that is not in the model's word
vocabulary. It may never have been seen in training, or it may have been dropped
from the vocabulary for a reason such as a frequency threshold. In languages
that produce many inflected forms, such as Turkish, the coverage of a word-level
vocabulary matters all the more. [↩](#term-out-of-vocabulary-oov){.term-back}
:::

For a form that is not in the word table — an [out-of-vocabulary](#gloss-out-of-vocabulary-oov){#term-out-of-vocabulary-oov .term-ref}
word — no row can be fetched directly. The `gensim` word-vector lookup used
here raises a `KeyError` in that case; other systems may use a special
unknown-unit representation. The variety of forms in Turkish makes this coverage
problem especially visible.

Here are two Wikipedia samples of comparable size, one Turkish and one
English:

```text
### corpora
  turkish   103040 lines    1458213 tokens    138578 types
  english    44079 lines    1828840 tokens     78140 types
```

Turkish produced **138,578 distinct word forms from 1.46 million tokens**;
English produced 78,140 from *more* tokens — 1.83 million. Turkish
agglutination means `ev`, `evim`, `evimde`, `evimdeki`, `evlerimizdekiler`
are five separate entries in a word-level vocabulary, each needing its own
vector, each estimated from its own sparse handful of occurrences.

```text
### vocabulary growth: new word forms per million tokens
  turkish  250k:45688  500k:73435  750k:97412  1000k:112644  1250k:126389
  english  250k:22869  500k:34016  750k:42854  1000k:52347  1250k:60178

### the tail: how much of the vocabulary is seen exactly once
  turkish   50.0% of types are hapax (69296 of 138578)
  english   46.7% of types are hapax (36503 of 78140)

### out-of-vocabulary rate: train on 90%, test on the last 10%
  turkish   7.33% of tokens unseen, 28.99% of types unseen
  english   4.72% of tokens unseen, 23.29% of types unseen
```

In this sample one million tokens contain 112,644 Turkish forms and 52,347
English forms, and new forms keep arriving over the range shown. In the held-out
Turkish portion about one token in fourteen falls outside the training
vocabulary. That about half the observed types occur once does not mean half
the vectors are learned from a single example: a frequency filter can leave
those types out, and a single token can produce several context pairs. These
numbers belong to one sample, one tokenization choice and one way of choosing
the held-out portion; they change on another sample.

::: {#gloss-subword .column-margin .term-gloss}
**subword** — a piece smaller than a word. Storing pieces instead of whole
words means an unseen word can still be assembled from parts you do know. [↩](#term-subword){.term-back}
:::

fastText's answer [@bojanowski2017enriching] is to stop treating a word as
atomic. Represent it as the sum of its character n-grams — its [subwords](#gloss-subword){#term-subword .term-ref} —
plus a vector for the whole word:

$$
\mathbf{v}_w = \mathbf{1}_{\{w \in \mathcal{V}\}}\,\mathbf{z}_w
+ \sum_{g \in G(w)} \mathbf{z}_g
$$

Here $\mathcal{V}$ is the whole-word vocabulary and $G(w)$ is the multiset of
the selected character n-grams. The separate whole-word component exists only
for words in the vocabulary; an out-of-vocabulary word is built from its
subword components. The sum describes the composition used in training; how the
exported vector is scaled depends on the implementation.

Shared character n-grams can receive updates from examples in different words:
`<pu` is also contained in `pump`, `pumps`, `pumped`, `pumping` and `punch`.
That lets rare words benefit from forms that are seen more often. Not every
piece is learned from plentiful data, however. fastText maps the n-grams to a
fixed number of hash-table buckets, and different pieces can share a bucket.
That a vector can be produced for an out-of-vocabulary word does not by itself
show that the vector is semantically reliable.

The sum in the paper and the mean of the same learned components, divided by
their number (what the `fastText` and `gensim` implementations do), give the
same direction for a non-zero word vector; the word-to-word cosines of the two
versions are identical. That should not be read as saying that using a sum or a
mean in training, or combining different words into a document vector, is
equivalent under all conditions.

::: {.column-margin}
Shared n-gram vectors tie together the representations of words that are spelled
alike. That trade-off can provide morphological generalization, and it can also
create unwanted closeness between unrelated words. The separate whole-word
component of an in-vocabulary word can learn information apart from that
effect. The contribution of a given n-gram is shared among the words that
contain it.
:::

::: {.fig-cap}
Every word is a bag of character n-grams plus, if the model ever saw it, the
word itself. Rare and unseen words are no longer a special case — which is
why this is the default choice for morphologically rich languages like
Turkish. Drawn with 3-grams so it stays readable; fastText's default is every
n-gram of length 3 to 6, so a real `pumpage` decomposes into 22 pieces, not 7.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ftWord = Inputs.text({
  label: "Word", value: "kitaplarımızdaki",
  placeholder: "try: evlerimizde, pumping, cavitation", width: 320
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ftN = Inputs.range([3, 6], {label: "n-gram size", step: 1, value: 4})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ftGrams = {
  const token = (ftWord || "").toLowerCase().trim();
  if (!token || /\s/u.test(token)) return [];
  const chars = Array.from("<" + token + ">");
  return Array.from({length: Math.max(0, chars.length - ftN + 1)},
    (_, i) => chars.slice(i, i + ftN).join(""));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ftOther = Inputs.text({label: "Compare with", value: "kitaplar", width: 320})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ftShared = {
  const token = (ftOther || "").toLowerCase().trim();
  if (!token || /\s/u.test(token)) return new Set();
  const chars = Array.from("<" + token + ">");
  return new Set(Array.from({length: Math.max(0, chars.length - ftN + 1)},
    (_, i) => chars.slice(i, i + ftN).join("")));
}
```


Trained on the same Turkish Wikipedia sample, word2vec and fastText behave
very differently on words the corpus never contained:

```text
### a word the corpus never saw
  kitaplarımızdaki   in word2vec vocab: False   in fastText vocab: False
    fastText still answers: kitapları 0.91, kitapların 0.91, kitaplıkları 0.90, kitaplarda 0.90
    word2vec raises: KeyError
  bilgisayarcılık    in word2vec vocab: False   in fastText vocab: False
    fastText still answers: bilgisayara 0.96, bilgisayarlı 0.96, bilgisayar 0.96, bilgisayarı 0.96
    word2vec raises: KeyError
```

Shared character pieces can be useful for some typos as well. In the examples
below the out-of-vocabulary forms get vectors close to the expected words; that
result is not guaranteed for every typo.

```text
  philosphy       in vocab: False
    philosophy 0.96, philosophie 0.95, philosophies 0.94, philology 0.94, philo 0.93
  governmentt     in vocab: False
    government 0.98, governments 0.94, governmental 0.93, governs 0.91, govern 0.91
```

### The price of subwords

Character n-grams make it possible to share some stem and suffix patterns
without an explicit morphological analyser. In return, the representations of
words that are spelled alike but mean different things can move closer together
too.

```text
### morphology: does fastText put inflected forms together?
  ft  kitap    kitapta 0.96, kitaba 0.95, kitab 0.94, kitabın 0.94, kitabı 0.93
  w2v kitap    eseri 0.81, makale 0.80, eseriyle 0.80, kitabın 0.80, kitaplar 0.79

  ft  yaz      yao 0.78, yağ 0.77, yağdı 0.77, yayoi 0.76, yay 0.75
  w2v yaz      kış 0.86, olimpiyatları 0.84, aylarında 0.83, gündönümü 0.80
```

For `kitap` (book), fastText returns inflections of `kitap`; word2vec returns
`eseri` (his/her work), `makale` (article) — *semantic* neighbours. Which one
you want depends entirely on your task.

In this run the word2vec neighbours of `yaz` (summer, and also "write") reflect
the seasonal usage more: `kış` (winter), `olimpiyatları` (olympics),
`gündönümü` (solstice). In the fastText list, forms with similar spelling come
to the front: `yao`, `yağ` (oil), `yayoi`, `yay` (bow). The observation shows
that sharing characters can create unwanted closeness. To say that the
difference comes only from the word being three letters long, however, one
would have to compare n-gram settings, frequency and different training seeds.

```text
### the price, measured
  kitap    kitle    fastText +0.667   word2vec +0.446
```

In this example the cosine of `kitap` (book) and `kitle` (mass, crowd) is 0.667
in fastText and 0.446 in word2vec. The cosine distributions of the two spaces
can differ, so the ratio cannot be read as "half again as much semantic
similarity". The score distributions of unrelated or hard-negative pairs would
have to be compared as well.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**The rule to remember.** fastText is a strong candidate for tasks where
out-of-vocabulary forms and inflectional variety matter. Character sharing can
also create unwanted closeness, however; evaluate the method by coverage and by
task performance, not by accepting or rejecting it unconditionally according to
word length. The idea it shares with the BPE of @sec-text-as-data is to benefit
from rare wholes through their pieces. The mechanism differs: BPE determines the
tokenization units, whereas fastText builds a word vector by combining the
vectors of overlapping character n-grams.
:::

## Documents as vectors

@sec-text-as-data classified 20 Newsgroups posts with TF-IDF. Now we have
word vectors — do they help? The question is how to produce a coordinate for a
*document* when what we have is a coordinate per word. The obvious answer is
the mean, the centroid of the word vectors in a document, which gives a
100-dimensional document vector instead of a 32,000-dimensional sparse one.

```python
def average(docs):
    # docs: a list of documents, each one a list of tokens (not a raw string).
    # Out-of-vocabulary tokens are skipped; a document with no vector stays a zero row.
    out = np.zeros((len(docs), g.vector_size), dtype=np.float32)
    for i, tokens in enumerate(docs):
        if isinstance(tokens, str):
            raise TypeError("each document must be a list of tokens, not a raw string")
        vs = [g[w] for w in tokens if w in g.key_to_index]
        if vs:
            out[i] = np.mean(vs, axis=0)
    return out
```

Tokenization and case conversion have to be applied consistently to the
training and the test documents. Cosine similarity is undefined for zero
vectors, so a search application also needs an explicit empty-representation
rule. In the experiment below, 79 of the 2,327 training documents and 65 of the
1,550 test documents stay zero rows.

A step up from the plain mean is to weight it by IDF:

$$
\mathbf{v}_d = \frac{\sum_{i \in I_d} \mathrm{idf}(w_i)\, \mathbf{v}_{w_i}}
                    {\sum_{i \in I_d} \mathrm{idf}(w_i)}
$$

Here $I_d$ is the set of token positions in the document that have a word
vector; repeated words contribute at every position. IDF is computed from the
training documents only and held fixed at test time. If the denominator is zero,
an explicit empty-representation rule applies, as for the plain mean. As in
@sec-text-as-data, this weighting reduces the relative contribution of words
that occur in many documents. The variant appears in the table below as
`idf-weighted averaged glove`.

doc2vec [@le2014distributed] assigns a learnable vector to the document id as
well. Training is based on predicting target words; output objectives such as
negative sampling or hierarchical softmax can be used. It has two basic
architectures:

| Variant | Input | Predicts |
|---|---|---|
| **PV-DM** | document vector + context words | the target word |
| **PV-DBOW** | the document vector alone | words sampled from the document |

: The two doc2vec variants {tbl-colwidths="[22,44,34]"}

Loosely, they are the CBOW and skip-gram of the document world — the
input–output columns show they are not literally the same models.

::: {.column-margin}
The original work favours PV-DM, while @lau2016empirical found that PV-DBOW can
also be strong, and computationally convenient, on the tasks they examined. In
`gensim`, `dm=1` (the default) selects PV-DM and `dm=0` selects PV-DBOW. On
reproducibility, a follow-up written with one of the original authors is
instructive ([Mesnil et al., 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.5335)). Its final
version (v7) reports 88.73% accuracy with paragraph vectors alone, against the
92.58% IMDB accuracy (7.42% error) of the original paper, and states that 92.6%
appeared only when the training and test data were *not shuffled*. That is the
result of one particular replication; it is not a verdict on every replication
of the method.
:::

Every training document is assigned a learnable vector. For a new document the
model's word and output parameters are held fixed and the new document vector is

computation is an important difference from averaging word vectors directly.

Same four categories, same train/test split, same logistic regression on top.

```text
### documents as vectors: five representations
tf-idf (chapter 2 baseline)        accuracy 0.853   dimensions   32014
averaged glove                     accuracy 0.820   dimensions     100
idf-weighted averaged glove        accuracy 0.822   dimensions     100
doc2vec (PV-DBOW, 40 epochs)       accuracy 0.839   dimensions     100
averaged glove + doc2vec           accuracy 0.845   dimensions     200
```

A single accuracy computed from 1,550 documents carries uncertainty. For example,
the standard error of an accuracy near 0.83 is about 0.010 under the binomial
approximation; that value is not, however, the standard error of the difference
between the accuracies of two models. To decide whether gaps of 0.2, 1.9 or 3.3
points are significant, the predictions on the same documents have to be
examined as pairs and, where possible, results reported on different splits.
The note below gives that paired comparison.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Advanced evaluation note: comparing two representations on the same documents

McNemar's test can be used to compare the accuracies of two models that
classify the same test documents. The test compares the counts, in the two
directions, of documents that one model gets right and the other gets wrong.
Predicting different wrong classes does not by itself enter that disagreement.
An effect size and a paired uncertainty interval should be reported too, and
the variability across different splits examined separately.

The counts measured on this split:

| Comparison | Only the first right | Only the second right | Exact McNemar $p$ |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| TF-IDF – averaged GloVe | 135 | 84 | 0.0007 |
| TF-IDF – IDF-weighted averaged GloVe | 129 | 81 | 0.0011 |
| IDF-weighted – plain averaged GloVe | 66 | 63 | 0.86 |

: Paired comparison on the same 1,550 test documents {tbl-colwidths="[40,20,22,18]"}

The Bonferroni threshold for three comparisons is $0.05 / 3 \approx 0.017$; the
first two differences fall below it and the 0.2-point gap between the two GloVe
averages does not. We cannot give the same calculation for the doc2vec rows:
`gensim`'s `infer_vector` derives its starting vector from a hash value that
changes in every Python session, so the doc2vec predictions behind the table
cannot be reproduced exactly. With a fixed hash, the chapter notebook finds
doc2vec accuracies between 0.830 and 0.836 over three seeds.
:::

On this split the highest accuracy is in the TF-IDF row. The dense
representations reach accuracies close to the 32,014-dimensional sparse one
using 100 or 200 coordinates. The paired predictions show that the gap between
TF-IDF and the two GloVe averages is hard to explain by chance on this split
(the note above); the same calculation could not be made for the gaps to the
doc2vec rows. A reduction in the number of coordinates does not translate
directly into the same ratio of memory saved; sparse storage, running time and
the search method to be used have to be measured as well. A small
classification task and large-scale document search can call for different
choices.

::: {.column-margin}
In topic classification the mean of the word vectors can be a useful starting
representation. The SIF approach of @arora2017simple uses weights
$a / (a + p(w))$ that depend on word frequency and removes a common dominant
component. That is not the same method as the IDF-weighted mean above; it is a
separate baseline that can be compared on tasks such as sentence similarity.
:::

Two more measurements before leaving this. First, coverage:

```text
### coverage: how much of the corpus does glove actually know?
  tokens covered: 98.6%
  types covered : 84.5%  (23395 of 27681)
```

In this measurement GloVe covers 98.6% of the tokens and 84.5% of the types. The
forms it does not cover make up 1.4% of the token mass, which shows that the
group is rare overall. How many of them are typos, proper names or domain terms
has to be examined separately. The averaging method used here leaves those
forms out.

Second, the failure that no amount of averaging can fix:

```python
a = "the pump failed and the valve is fine".split()
b = "the valve failed and the pump is fine".split()
va = np.mean([g[w] for w in a], axis=0)
vb = np.mean([g[w] for w in b], axis=0)
```

```text
### what averaging destroys
  cosine of the two averaged vectors: 1.0000
  identical: True
```

The same tokens occur the same number of times in the two sentences, so the
unordered mean is mathematically the same vector. In floating-point arithmetic
the order of addition can produce very small rounding differences; bit-level
equality is not guaranteed in every implementation. The `identical: True` here
is the result of an `np.allclose` comparison; in the same run the bit-level
comparison (`np.array_equal`) gives `False`, and the largest difference is
$1.2 \times 10^{-7}$. The basic limitation does not change: averaging does not
keep the word order that determines which part failed. This is chapter 2's
bag-of-words problem, now with 100 dimensions instead of 32,000.

Word order needs a model that reads the sequence. That is @sec-language-models
and @sec-transformers.

## The geometry has problems

Reading static embeddings means keeping distributional relatedness, the
distribution of directions and the effect of frequency apart. After that we
look at the arbitrariness of the coordinate system and at how consistent
different training runs are.

### In this space, cosine reflects relatedness more than similarity

```text
  good       bad        0.770
  hot        cold       0.725
  increase   decrease   0.881
  cat        dog        0.880
  cat        car        0.311
  teacher    student    0.808
```

The pair `increase`–`decrease` scores 0.881 and the pair `cat`–`dog` 0.880. We
do not have enough evidence to read that small difference as a meaningful
ordering. The important observation here is that the antonym pair gets a high
cosine value too.

This is not a bug in GloVe; it is the distributional hypothesis doing exactly
what it promised. Antonyms are largely substitutable in context — *sales
increased sharply* and *sales decreased sharply* are both fluent — so they
keep identical company and land in the same place.

This is called the **antonym problem**, and its one-sentence definition is:
[words with *opposite* meanings do not sit far apart in embedding space; they
sit close together.]{.hl} Take `hot` and `cold`. Intuition says "opposite
meaning, opposite direction"; but the model never sees meaning, only which
words appear around a word. `hot` and `cold` both appear next to `water`,
`weather`, `very`, `too` — almost the same circle of friends — and to the
model, having the same circle is what being close means. The practical cost: a
system searching for "hot" may return documents containing "cold" among its
most similar results.

Task-specific labels, for contradiction or synonymy for example, can help a
model learn this distinction, and what is learned can generalize to pairs that
were not seen directly in training. Success still depends on the coverage of
the data and on the training objective; using such labels does not by itself
guarantee that every antonym pair will be separated.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**The rule to remember.** Words that keep the same company end up close
distributionally, so proximity does not mean synonymy. Cosine itself is a
geometric measure — what it carries depends on the objective that trained the
embedding. In this space it mostly carries *relatedness*, and similarity and
oppositeness are both kinds of it.
:::

@steck2024cosine show that, in certain linear matrix-factorization models, the
cosines can change while the training predictions are preserved. The result
draws attention to the fact that cosine is not a scale of meaning independent of
the learned representation. The distribution over random pairs gives a useful
basis for comparison; assessing similarity for a task additionally requires
suitable labelled examples. Do not treat a value of 0.8 in two models as
directly equivalent.

**Do not read the raw cosine of static vectors directly as a measure of sentiment
or polarity.** Evaluation data measure different relations as well: WordSim-353
[@finkelstein2002placing] contains judgements that also reflect broad semantic
relatedness, whereas SimLex-999 [@hill2015simlex], developed later, specifically
aims to separate similarity from relatedness. The scores models get on the two
sets come up in the evaluation section.

### The space is not isotropic

The word itself first. **Isotropic** means "the same in every direction".
Picture every word vector as an arrow leaving a common centre. In an isotropic
space those arrows spread evenly in all directions, like the spines of a
hedgehog: as many point north as south, as many up as down. Pick two arrows at
random and the angle between them is, on average, a right angle, so their
cosine averages zero. That is what we expect of "two unrelated words".

**Anisotropic** is the opposite: the arrows are not spread evenly; most of
them lean the same way — like stalks of wheat bent one way by the wind. In
such a space even two random arrows are somewhat alike; the angle between them
is narrower than a right angle and their cosine averages above zero.

It matters because it moves the *zero point* of cosine. In an isotropic space
a cosine of 0.3 says "these two words are related"; in an anisotropic one the
same 0.3 can be an ordinary value that completely unrelated pairs get too. So
before you interpret a cosine you need to know what random pairs score in that
space. Let us measure that for ours.

```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
M = g.get_normed_vectors()                       # (400000, 100), unit rows
sample = rng.choice(50_000, size=4000, replace=False)   # top 50k only
S = M[sample]
vals = (S @ S.T)[np.triu_indices(4000, k=1)]
```

```text
  mean cosine between random word pairs : 0.029
  std                                   : 0.119
  share of pairs with cosine > 0        : 56.9%
  norm of the mean vector               : 0.171
  after subtracting the mean, mean cosine: -0.000
```

In this space a shared dominant direction has formed that many vectors
project onto strongly: most words lean somewhat the same way, and 56.9% of
random pairs have positive cosine. "Every vector has the same component" would
be too strong — this is a tendency, not a rule that holds vector by vector.
The size of the tendency is *measurable*, though: the mean vector has norm
0.171, and removing it leaves a mean cosine of zero. The practical consequence: do not read raw cosine values as if they were
on the same scale across models.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: the isotropic null and the mean-vector norm

Be precise about the null, because the obvious phrasing is wrong: for
independent unit vectors drawn uniformly in $d$ dimensions the angles do *not*
spread evenly — they concentrate near 90°, with mean cosine 0 and variance
$1/d$. Isotropy means no direction is special, not that every angle is equally
likely.

The 56.9% figure proves little on its own: under an isotropic null the share
would be 50%, and the 8 million pairs behind it come from 4,000 vectors, so
they are nowhere near independent observations.

Nor are the mean cosine and the mean-vector norm two separate pieces of
evidence. For $n$ unit vectors they are the same number:
$\bar{c} = (n\lVert\bar{v}\rVert^2 - 1)/(n-1)$, and
$(4000 \times 0.171^2 - 1)/3999 = 0.029$ exactly — a real finding, and a milder
one than a narrow cone. At a mean cosine of 0.029 the vectors are not crammed
into a sliver of the sphere; they are tilted off centre. Note also what centring
does not buy: a zero mean removes the shared direction, it does not make the
covariance spherical.
:::

Subtracting the mean vector (centring) reduces most of it, and removing the
top few principal components as well reduces more; @mu2018allbutthetop showed
this costs one line of code and improves most similarity benchmarks. Read
these as *mitigations*, not as a *cure*: depending on the task, centring or
whitening can help, but the directions you throw away sometimes carry useful
information and go with them. Measure on your own task before and after. The problem
does not go away in modern models — @ethayarajh2019contextual found that
contextual embeddings from BERT and GPT-2 are *more* anisotropic than static
ones, not less.

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Cosine between 8 million random word pairs, before and after removing the mean</div>
```
